title: AI at Honeycomb: What’s Actually Working (w/ CTO Charity Majors)
summary: Honeycomb CTO Charity Majors says AI has modestly changed team velocity, speeds up throwaway prototyping more than core systems, and that communication and production feedback still matter most.

assertions.quote: it hasn't transformed our team's velocity. It's made us a little slower in some places, a little faster in others.

verdicts.note: The Stanford 100k-developer study and other field data put average gains around 10-20%, far below 2x-10x marketing claims.

Google RCT, 96 full-time engineers on an enterprise-grade C++ task in the monorepo: AI cut time on task by ~21% in the best-fit model (95% CI crosses zero, p=0.086), well below Peng et al.'s 56% and in line with Cui et al.'s 26%.

Field RCTs with 4,867 developers at Microsoft, Accenture and a Fortune-100 firm: Copilot raised weekly completed PRs by 26% (SE 10.3%), substantially smaller than the lab's 56% speedup, which the authors attribute to real work being less assistable.

METR 2025: in large, mature repos (~10 years old, >1.1M LOC) AI helped less than in greenfield RCTs, and on average slowed developers by 19%; this goes beyond 'modest gains', and the repos are open-source rather than enterprise.

Google reports large end-to-end savings (about 50% on int64, about 89% on small Joda clusters) in a 500M+ LOC codebase, but only for bespoke migration pipelines with fine-tuned models, not average developer work, and the figures are engineers' estimates.

Field DID at a 5,000-person IT services firm (201 devs, 27 weeks, 2023-24 Copilot/ChatGPT/Gemini): AI users completed 1.08 more user stories per week (+18%), a real gain but modest next to 55% or 10x headlines; usage was self-reported and partly self-selected.

assertions.quote: the ideation phase when when you're throwing a lot of code away anyway has gotten a lot faster.

verdicts.note: Direction is well supported: greenfield, low-stakes work gets the biggest gains in studies and surveys. The specific multipliers are anecdote.

METR 2025 caveat: its slowdown on mature repos is 'consistent with small greenfield projects or development in unfamiliar codebases seeing substantial speedup'. This is a hypothesis; prototyping was not measured.

assertions.quote: database engineers who are working on storage engine it has not transformed their velocity and nor should it

verdicts.note: Consistent across Stanford's data, METR's mature-repo slowdown and long-context degradation results.

Google's complex enterprise task (unfamiliar 474-line CL, build/test updates) yielded ~21% vs 56% on Peng's simple HTTP-server task, but the authors attribute the gap mainly to population differences rather than task complexity.

Comparing two separate experiments: the AI accuracy gain fell on harder tasks (0.124 vs 0.264), but the task-count gain rose slightly (0.283 vs 0.245). Complexity was not manipulated, and the authors call this suggestive.

assertions.quote: our our designers can you know uh do do code prototypes

verdicts.note: Tools like Lovable, v0, Replit let non-developers produce working prototypes; widely observed.

assertions.quote: any engineer who can tell me what they want to do and why is more than capable of you know generating the code

verdicts.note: Requirements, stakeholder alignment and judgment remain hard to delegate; plausible though not strictly testable.

assertions.quote: Doesn't matter how fast you're going if you aren't working on things that really change your users's lives.

verdicts.note: Plausible economic logic and widely argued, but not measured; execution, distribution and maintenance still matter.

assertions.quote: the world of software is bifurcating into disposable software stuff that nobody really understands

verdicts.note: A framing of how software is changing rather than a measurable claim.
